snippet.title: The Strange Algorithm People Used To Run Their Lives
snippet.description:
The  1970s were a decade packed with real scientific breakthroughs; NASA launched Voyager 1, Intel revolutionized computing with the first microprocessor, and JVC introduced the VHS. At the same time, some more -- shall we say -- outside-the-box ideas also started quietly gaining traction, ideas like biorhythms. Promoted as a scientific way to predict your physical, emotional, and intellectual highs and lows, biorhythms captured the public's imagination... but were they really all that?

On this episode of Weird History, we dive into one of the strangest fads of the seventies' new age movement and try to determine whether it was legit science or just pseudoscience dressed up in math. 

And have you ever had a biorhythm reading? Let us know in the comments!

snippet.title: What is "The Thinker" actually thinking about? - Noah Charney
snippet.description:
Get to know Auguste Rodin’s infamous sculpture “The Thinker,” and find out who was the inspiration for this masterpiece.

--

Contrary to popular belief, "The Thinker" sculpture isn’t just a universal symbol of eternal contemplation. French sculptor Auguste Rodin intended it to represent a specific person— and fit into a much larger piece featuring the fiery pits of Hell. So, who was "The Thinker," and what was he actually thinking? Noah Charney digs into the secrets of this infamous work of art.

snippet.description:
Why Was Anubis Guarding This Shrine?

Ancient Egyptians never placed anything by accident.

Anubis wasn’t simply decorating Tutankhamun’s tomb. He was positioned above this shrine as its eternal guardian. Some believe he protected sacred ritual equipment, while others imagine lost documents filled with ancient knowledge. Archaeology supports the first explanation, while the second remains an intriguing theory without evidence.

Which explanation makes more sense to you?

snippet.title: What Was It Like Being A Monk During the Black Death? | Medieval London 1348 | Day 2 of 7
snippet.description:
Forty percent of England's clergy were dead by the end of 1349.

Not fled. Not retired. Dead. The monks and priests who went into the infected houses — who held the hands of the dying, administered last rites, heard confessions in rooms where every breath was a risk — died at twice the rate of the general population. The people most obligated to stay were the people most likely to die for staying.

This is Day 2 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a Benedictine monk at Westminster Abbey, November 1348. You wake up at two in the morning for Matins. You pray seven times a day, every day, without exception. You tend to the dying in the infirmary with treatments you suspect are not working. You sit beside a brother who has been here for twenty years and sing psalms with him while he is still able to move his lips.

And this afternoon, a letter arrives from the Bishop of London that has never been sent before in the history of the English church — because there are simply not enough priests left to do what priests are supposed to do.

The Rule of Saint Benedict was written for exactly this. For the moments when everything wants you to stop, go quiet, and retreat into private grief. The Rule says: get up. Say the office. Come back tomorrow.

Using AI trained on monastic records, medieval chronicles, and the actual canonical hours of Benedictine life, we've reconstructed what one day inside Westminster Abbey actually looked like in November 1348.

His mother rushed him to Paris for an experimental vaccine from Louis Pasteur, and he became the first rabies-vaccinated person to survive. localized.description:
Take a look at what makes rabies the most lethal infectious disease, and what measures you should take if you're exposed to it.

--

In 1885, Joseph Meister was bit in 14 places by a rabid dog. His mother rushed him to Paris for an experimental vaccine from Louis Pasteur, and he became the first rabies-vaccinated person to survive. Today, without proper intervention, rabies remains deadly in almost all cases. So, what makes it so dangerous to humans? Charles Rupprecht explores what makes this infectious disease so lethal.

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Apprentice (Black Death) | day 1 of 7
snippet.description:
It is November 1348. London has 80,000 people. The plague arrived three weeks ago.

Nobody is talking about it. Not openly. Not yet.

This is Day 1 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a 16-year-old apprentice on Cheapside — the loudest, busiest, most extraordinary street in medieval England. You sleep on a straw pallet on your master's workshop floor. You eat dark gritty bread and small ale for breakfast. You carry bolts of broadcloth through streets named after the things they sell — Bread Street, Milk Street, Honey Lane, Goldsmiths Row.

And this morning, on an errand near St Mary-le-Bow, you see something in a churchyard that you cannot stop thinking about.

The swellings have started. The bells are ringing more than usual. Your master burns rosemary in the doorway and tells you not to linger in crowds. The city is going about its ordinary business. And somewhere underneath the noise of Cheapside, something is very wrong.

Using AI trained on medieval chronicles, guild records, and archaeological evidence, we've reconstructed what one ordinary day in London looked like in the last week before everything changed.

snippet.title: Why This Princess's Life Was No Fairy Tale
snippet.description:
Princess Diana was one of the most beloved and iconic royals in modern history. But behind the fairy-tale image, lies a far darker story. snippet.title: What Did New York Look Like in 1650? (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
What did New York City look like in 1650 — before the skyscrapers, before the grid, before any of it?
Most people have never seen it. Not really.
Using advanced AI reconstruction built on historical maps, colonial records, and archaeological research, we travel back to a time when Manhattan was still a small Dutch outpost called New Amsterdam — a muddy, windswept trading post at the edge of the known world, clinging to the southern tip of an island most Europeans had never heard of.
No skyscrapers. No subway. No crowds.
Just dirt paths through marshland, wooden houses facing the harbor, a half-built fort, a single canal, and about 1,000 people trying to make a life at the bottom of an island that would one day hold 8 million.
This video brings that world back to life — not as paintings, not as old maps — but as a fully immersive, cinematic reconstruction of what New Amsterdam may have actually looked and felt like nearly 400 years ago.

🕰️ What you'll discover:

New Amsterdam in 1650 — the real layout, streets, and skyline
Daily life inside one of the first European settlements in North America
The original landscape of Manhattan before it was reshaped
The Dutch trading culture that quietly laid the foundations of New York City
How a tiny colonial outpost became one of the most powerful cities in history
